summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Boyacá. A visitor to the department is assessed against Colombia's national framework and the national pattern of anti-trans violence, with incidents from other departments cited only as evidence of how that pattern expresses itself.

Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, attacked in Bello, Antioquia; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon. No arrests have been made, though police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Caquetá, armed groups distributed "social cleansing" flyers naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, was given one week by three armed men to leave town or be killed and fled at night after hiding for a week. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024. Discrimination limits trans women in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Couples married abroad involving a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
The incidents documented in the source inventory occurred in Antioquia and Caquetá, not Boyacá, and are cited as evidence of the national pattern rather than as department-specific risk. Boyacá's own record contains no comparable documentation of armed-group flyer campaigns, forced displacement of trans residents, or targeted killings.

Colombia's decades-long civil conflict continues to shape the environment: armed groups operating despite the 2016 peace agreement drive the organised "social cleansing" campaigns recorded in Caquetá and, separately, kill lists posted in Guajira since March 2024. Whether comparable armed-group presence affects Boyacá is not addressed in the sources.
